claims.text: High-temperature structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys is primarily governed by configurational entropy.
Configurational entropy suppresses phase segregation relative to low-entropy alloys with similar compositions.
Configurational entropy suppresses atomic diffusion relative to low-entropy alloys with similar compositions.
The proposed high-entropy nanoalloys contain at least five metallic elements in near-equiatomic ratios.
The initial high-entropy nanoalloy is a single-phase solid solution.
High configurational entropy increases the energy barrier for atomic rearrangement.
An increased barrier to atomic rearrangement stabilizes the single-phase structure and inhibits phase separation.
The proposed entropy-mediated barrier reduces segregation and diffusion-driven coarsening.
After high-temperature annealing, high-entropy nanoalloys will retain a single-phase structure and homogeneous elemental distribution.
High-entropy nanoalloys will undergo less grain growth than low-entropy nanoalloys under identical annealing conditions.
High-entropy nanoalloys will undergo less phase separation than low-entropy nanoalloys under identical annealing conditions.
Differences in phase stability and elemental homogeneity can be observed using XRD and EDS mapping.
Binary or ternary nanoalloy controls are expected to exhibit significant phase segregation and coarsening under the same annealing conditions.
The prediction is restricted to nanoalloys having at least five near-equiatomic elements and annealed above 800°C for no more than 24 hours.
The prediction does not cover particles smaller than 5 nm, reactive-gas environments, or highly immiscible element combinations.
